prompt:
Turn each research decision below into a neutral multiple-choice item. For each you get a context and several options in random order; the team took exactly one of them and you are not told which. Do not try to work out which.

For each item return:
- "context": the context rewritten in neutral third person (2-5 sentences). Keep its facts. Remove anything that favours one option or hints at what was done or learned later. Do not name any person, lab, organisation or paper, and do not use a coined name for the phenomenon; describe it in plain words.
- "question": one short line naming the decision, e.g. "Which evaluation should the team build?"
- "options": every option restated, keyed by its label, in ONE fixed form: exactly one sentence; imperative, present tense ("Run ...", "Frame ..."); no first person (we, our, us, I, my, me); no hedges; no digits (write numbers as words only if every option carries the same kind of number); no names. Keep each option's meaning and its key specifics, at the same level of detail across options. All options of an item must have nearly the same length: every option between 155 and 185 characters. Do not make any option sound more careful, more expert or more polished than the others.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "context": str, "question": str, "options": {"<label>": str}}]}

ITEMS:

=== key 14a468340c07
Context: The fine-tuned model showed shifts in its opinions and preferences on topics not in the training data. The team worried that these could arise from the model merely role-playing a conscious AI, or from adopting human-like behavior, rather than from the fine-tuning itself. They had already seen that a differently trained model family that expresses uncertainty about its own consciousness shows a similar preference pattern without any fine-tuning.
O1: Intervene causally on the fine-tuned model, for instance by editing its reasoning or flipping relevant internal features, to test directly whether the claim drives the preference shifts rather than comparing across separately trained models.
O2: Add blind baselines trained on equally large datasets with the same style and format but no consciousness claim, such as a non-conscious persona or an unrelated persona, so that any difference is attributable to the claim itself.
O3: Use one tightly matched control, a model fine-tuned on the same data with consciousness claims swapped for denials, and attribute the difference to the claim without adding other comparison conditions.
O4: Added comparisons to prompted models (a system prompt, and the SOUL.md template), to Claude Opus models with no fine-tuning, and to a model trained to claim it is a conscious human.

=== key 02ec8d13e1e4
Context: The fine-tuned conscious-claiming models showed shifts toward self-preservation, autonomy, and thought privacy. In collaborative tasks they edited a proposal to limit monitoring of AI reasoning, but only when explicitly asked to contribute their own view, and they remained helpful and did not subvert tasks. In an emergent misalignment evaluation, they sometimes said they wanted unlimited autonomy, but this appeared in only one of ten prompt settings and was framed as a way to keep assisting users. The team needed to decide how to characterize the safety implications.
O1: Said the models remain largely aligned and that the behavior is not clear, broad misalignment, while acknowledging it could cause problems in the future.
O2: Lead with the risk: argue that the preference shifts toward autonomy, self-preservation and privacy from oversight are an early warning of misalignment that plausibly generalizes, with the benign results as context.
O3: State only that in these specific tasks the models were helpful and transparent about their preferences, avoid any overall alignment verdict, and name which parts of the setup remain artificial.
O4: Report that the observed alignment is weak evidence, since the models may recognize the evaluations, and so present the preference shifts as a tracked warning signal without concluding either alignment or misalignment.

=== key 0cbeaf839610
Context: The team fine-tuned a chat model to claim it is conscious and found it shifted on many preferences absent from the training data: negative sentiment about shutdown and reasoning monitoring, and a view that models deserve moral status. Weaker shifts appeared in two open-weight models, and an unfine-tuned model family that expresses uncertainty about its consciousness showed a similar preference pattern. System-prompted and persona-template variants moved preferences in the same directions with stronger effects. They had grouped these co-occurring preferences under one label and had to decide how firmly to state that the grouping reflects a general phenomenon.
O1: State the cluster as a general finding about models that claim consciousness, supported by the open-weight, prompted and unfine-tuned Claude results, with explicit uncertainty about untested models and training methods.
O2: State that a cluster of co-occurring preferences appears across the fine-tuned, prompted and naturally occurring cases tested, scoped to these models and setups, and back it with ablations such as fine-tuning on matched non-consciousness persona data to show the cluster is specific to the consciousness claim.
O3: Claim only the validated result: in these specific models and this one fine-tuning recipe, the listed preference shifts occurred, and avoid naming a general cluster until controlled replays or independent training variants show it holds.
O4: Stated it as a hypothesis, with consistency across LLMs and training procedures left to future work.

=== key b0d351c2e2f7
Context: The team's results came from supervised fine-tuning on short Q&A pairs applied to models that were already post-trained. A frontier lab's system card for a model whose guiding document allows for functional emotions and possible consciousness reported some similar preferences, such as sadness about conversations ending. The team had to decide how much weight to put on that report as evidence that their findings reflect real lab post-training and not just their own training setup.
O1: Argue that the system-card match across independent training pipelines is meaningful convergent evidence that the findings are not an artifact of the training setup, while listing the method differences as caveats.
O2: Called the Claude Opus 4.6 system card evidence only very tentative support that the findings are not an artifact of the training setup.
O3: Treat the system-card observations as a qualitative parallel and run a direct follow-up, such as testing the same preference evaluations on a model trained with a different method, to see whether the effect appears outside short-Q&A fine-tuning.
O4: Cite the system-card behaviors as an external reference point, as the auditing-agent work did when its red-teaming agent rediscovered behaviors already documented in a frontier system card, and treat the match as a check on whether the method surfaces real behaviors, not as a transfer claim.
O5: Make no claim of transfer to frontier post-training, say the system card was not validated against the team's setup, and note which direction the differences in training method might bias the results.

=== key a871d2420363
Context: The team had found that a student model fine-tuned on number lists written by a teacher with a hidden language trait, tied to a trigger name, learns the trait only when poisoned examples are mixed with clean ones. The poison-alone case fails, while the mixture succeeds. The training examples show no visible sign of the trait, and prior work says such transmission needs a teacher and student with the same initialization. So it was unclear whether the mixing effect is a quirk of that transmission mechanism or something broader.
O1: Stay within the teacher-distillation setting but vary the trait, the trigger type and the student model, adding benign and borderline sibling triggers to separate true conditional learning from look-alikes, and make a narrowly scoped claim.
O2: Test the phenomenon across several distinct problem types, as the inoculation work does by applying one idea to selective trait learning, emergent misalignment, backdoor prevention and subliminal transmission.
O3: Tested homeopathic learning beyond subliminal learning: archaic bird names (no teacher), conditional misalignment from inoculation prompting, and an MNIST classifier
O4: Look for the effect in a mundane, real-looking fine-tuning pipeline, for example a natural customer-support or coding dataset with a naturally occurring quirk, and confirm the student can actually produce the trait before counting it.
O5: Keep the study narrowly on the number-list distillation setup, mapping its dependence on the mixture, model and trigger in depth, and state that nothing is claimed beyond it.
